messages.subject: Calculating detection probability in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance list serve-
I have questions on how to calculate the probability of detection in MCDS=
.  There=E2=80=99s an older post relating to Distance 5, and I see that t=
he example in Distance 6 v2 is a corrected example using the Amakihi data=
set.  I=E2=80=99ve managed to reproduce detection probability curve from =
the Distance output of the user manual=E2=80=99s Amakihi example (with co=
rrections=E2=80=94see below), but this example does not include a covaria=
te=E2=80=A6.a similar Amakihi example in Marques et al.=E2=80=99s 2007 Au=
k manuscript demonstrates this sort of output with a MCDS model, but the =
covariates are a factor and a continuous, and so Distance automatically p=
rovides the factor-only output.  So, my first problem relates to my inabi=
lity to duplicate the results of the Amakihi example on p. 99 of the Dist=
ance 6 v2 user=E2=80=99s guide (=E2=80=98Calculating probability of detec=
tion=E2=80=99).  In the =E2=80=98key(10)=E2=80=99 section, I think the 35=
.36 is a typo and should read 35.46 (this is parameter A(1), p. 97).  For=
 the =E2=80=98series(10/82.5)=E2=80=99 calculation, I obtain 0.12233 inst=
ead of 0.1581, and for =E2=80=98series(0/82.5)=E2=80=99 I obtain 0.1497 i=
nstead of 0.199.  These discrepancies make very little difference in the =
overall result--g(10) using =E2=80=98my=E2=80=99 values is 0.9379, while =
on p. 99 g(10) is 0.928, rounded to 0.93).  But I=E2=80=99ve successfully=
 reproduced the curve in the output of the model in the Amakihi dataset, =
which makes me think that there may be some small problems with the numbe=
r crunching on p.99=E2=80=A6.or?  My second question relates to applying =
this to my scenario.  I want to derive probabilities at levels of one fac=
tor covariate while controlling for levels of another factor covariate.  =
My most highly-supported model (half-normal key with 2-term cosine adjust=
ment) includes a covariate for sex (3 levels; female, male, and unknown g=
ender) and site (4 sites).  I would like to calculate the detection proba=
bility for each level of sex while controlling for site (i.e., =E2=80=98a=
verage=E2=80=99 the sex-specific detection function across study sites). =
 To do this, I multiplied each site coefficient by .33 in the detection p=
robability formula.  Here=E2=80=99s an example of how I applied this appr=
oach to calculate s (scale parameter) in the half-normal key series:
88.46 * exp(-.66 + (.33)(-.19)+(.33)(.03)+(.33)(-.25)),
Where 88.46 is the intercept of the scale parameter, -.66 is the coeffici=
ent for females, and -.19, .03, and -.25 are the coefficients for sites 1=
, 2, and 3, respectively.  I used this value (39.97) as the value in the =
key series expansion.  I have made a plug-and-chug formula in excel that =
satisfactorily (seemingly) creates sex-specific curves =E2=80=98averaged=E2=
=80=99 by site.  Does this approach seem reasonable?  Thanks for insights=
 on both the example in the user=E2=80=99s manual and about my applicatio=
n.  My email is druth...@usgs.gov; I=E2=80=99m happy to summarize and r=
e-post whatever advice I find.  Cheers, Dan

--

messages.subject: partly obscured visibility
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
we have been running DISTANCE type steppe ungulate surveys (wild ass and goitered gazelles) in the Mongolian Gobi since 2003. There are lots of problems with meeting DISTANCE sampling requirements, but besides getting important qualitative data we would like to at least come up with an estimate of the magnitude of the population. We do have 9 years of transect data (4-6 surveys per year for pooled estimates) and also did a simultanious point count last summer (http://www.savethewildhorse.org/files/Downloads/PDF/Studien/2010_08_27_point%20count.pdf). Especially concerning the analysis of the later I have two main questions:

1)*Topography compromizes visibility independent of distance*: We have very good GIS coverage of our study area and can really characterize our survey points (and transects). One problem we have with the point count is that tophography did obscure part of the visibility radius. We did count animals up to a distance of 7000m and for example assuming a radius of 7000m as the potential maximal visibility area we on average can only see 80% and this value varies between 100-46% among the 50 survey points. [The same is true for the 40 transect lines, but here the variability among the transects is small and pretty much is 20%.] How do you address this problem in the DISTANCE sampling analysis? For the point counts would you reduce the effort value for each point accordingly? How would you acount for this in the transect approach - just add 20% to the final estimate?

2)*Survey points are hills/mountains*: We know that steppe ungulates basically avoid steep slopes and we can assume that observers are seen and pose a certain disturbance. We binned observations in 0-100m, 101-500m, 501-1000m, 1001-2000m, 2001-5000m, and 5000-7000m
We have no observations in our 0-100m distance bin and several hills spread well into the 500m zone. So far we have just pooled the 0-100 and 101-500m zone into one bin of 0-500m, but I wonder if it would not be necessary to actually left truncate until 500m? Or is there any possibility to treat points differently in this respect?

Looking forward to comments. Best,
Petra

--

messages.subject: WORKSHOPS: Distance sampling training, Tanzania
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance-sampling list,

Registration is now open for workshops in practical skills for
ecologists to be held in Arusha, Tanzania, between 9th and 24th June.  A summary
of the workshops are given below; more information is available at
http://www.tzcrc.org/skills/   Please direct any questions to
arushaskill...@gmail.com

The workshops are linked to the 2011 International Joint Meeting of the
Association for Tropical Biology and Society for Conservation Biology, to be
held in Arusha from 12-16th June. http://www.atbc-scbafrica2011.org/

Workshops:

Primer on Distance Sampling
6-8 June
The emphasis of the workshop will be on how to design a good survey, how to
collect good data and how to do preliminary analyses using pen and paper, a
calculator and a computer spreadsheet.
Target audience: Any wildlife biologist who wants to design, collect or analyze
distance sampling survey data. Complete beginners are very welcome. Those with
more experience may: (i) benefit from the refresher, (ii) learn something from
the detailed discussion of assumptions, how to meet them, and what happens if
things go wrong, (iii) be able to use the material as a basis for teaching others.
Cost US$150

Distance Sampling Survey Design and Analysis
9-11 June
This workshop will focus on how to analyze distance sampling data in the
software Distance, as well as covering more advanced aspects of survey design.
Target audience: People who are familiar with the concepts covered on the
previous workshop, and who want to analyze survey data using the program
Distance. Pre-requisites: Attendance at workshop 1, or familiarity with all of
the concepts covered on that workshop (see web site for details).
US$150

Introduction to GIS
9-11 June
Elements of GIS, creation of maps & integration of GPS data, spatial analysis.
Focusing on QGIS (a free GIS package), this 3 day course will give practical
skills in creating maps, understanding cartographic concepts, and basic analysis.
US$100 for sponsored attendees, US$30 for unfunded students.

Introduction to GIS (Repeat of above course)
17-19 June
As above

Introduction to statistical analysis with R
20-24 June
This course offers students the chance to learn basic statistical methods at the
same time as learning R. The course aims to give students confidence in their
ability to undertake basic statistical analysis, give an awareness of the ways
in which these models can be extended, and to provide basic competence in using R.
US$100 for sponsored attendees, $30 for unfunded students.

--

Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling

messages.subject: Bug in DISTANCE 6.0: Estimation of encounter rate variance
messages.subject_clean: Bug in DISTANCE 6.0: Estimation of encounter rate variance
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,=20

I found a reproducible bug in DISTANCE 6.0 (Release2) concerning the
estimation of encounter rate variance. The problem occurred when working =
with
my own datasets, but for the sake of simplicity I will explain it at the
"Point Transect Example"  dataset included in the sample projects =
collection
provided with the software.

=20

For the analytic estimation of encounter rate variance under the =
assumption
of random sampler placement two estimators are available: 1st the
Design-derived estimator P2 (Fewster et al. 2009, Web Appendix B, eq.24 =
),
2nd the model-derived estimator P3 (Fewster et al. 2009: Web Appendix B,
eq.25), which is equivalent to eq. 3.79 of Buckland et al. (2001:79).  =
From
DISTANCE 6.0 on, P2 is the default setting, whereas older Versions use =
P3 as
default.

Both estimators reduce to Estimator P1 (Fewster et al. 2009, Web =
Appendix B,
eq.23 ) if sampling effort is the same for all points (t_i =3D t for all =
i).
This is the case for the "Point Transect Example"  dataset. (Here =
sampling
effort is 1 for all points (t_i =3Dt=3D 1 for all i), so P1 could even =
be further
simplified by dropping t^2 in the denominator, but that's not really
important for the problem).=20

The gist of the matter is, that both estimators (P2 and P3) should lead =
to
exactly the same results in the case of this dataset - but they don't.

=20

When fitting  a half normal detection function without adjustment terms =
and
without truncation, I obtained the following values:

=20

Estimator                            |             n/k
%CV=20

---------------------------------------------------------------------

P2                                          |             4.80
3.75

P3                                          |             4.80
8.84

Bootstrap                           |

(999 resamples)               |             4.79                       =
8.44

=20

The variance of the object density var(D) is estimated by the delta =
method
(Seber 1982: 7-9), one component of this estimator is the variance of n,
which  can be estimated by eq. 3.79 of Buckland et al. (2001:79). =
Because
this equation is equivalent to the model-derived estimator P3 and =
therefore
P2 in the case of this dataset, also the estimation of var(D) is =
affected, as
can be seen below:

=20

Estimator                            |             D
%CV                     =20

---------------------------------------------------------------------

P2                                          |             79.63
9.68    =20

P3                                          |             79.63
12.56    =20

Bootstrap                           |                            =20

(999 resamples)               |             77.86                     =
14.60

=20

At a first glance, the results of P3 seem to be more convincing, because =
they
match the results obtained by bootstrapping. For being sure about that, =
I
wrote a SAS macro to calculate P2 and P3 outside of DISTANCE, for both
estimators I came to the same results as with P3 inside DISTANCE.

=20

I replicated the analysis explained above with three different datasets =
and
the results were all the same: My SAS macro and the DISTANCE Version of =
P3
lead to the same results, which matched the results obtained by
bootstrapping. The DISTANCE Version of P2 lead to much lower Variance in =
all
cases.

=20

I did not figure out yet, if the problem also occurs when working with =
line
transect data.

=20

This bug may figure out to be a serious problem for many DISTANCE users =
as it
occurs when working with the default settings and affects the estimation =
of
precision. So can anybody please check my calculations, to be sure that =
I did
not make a mistake?!

=20

=20

Kind regards,=20

Tim

=20

=20

--

Tim Ritter, M.Sc.

=20

Georg-August-Universit=E4t

Abteilung =D6koinformatik, Biometrie und Waldwachstum

=20

Georg-August-University

Department Ecoinformatics, Biometrics and Forest Growth=20

B=FCsgenweg 4

37077 G=F6ttingen

GERMANY
